subject: geography
topicDisplay: Coastal Landscapes Glaciated Landscapes Dryland Landscapes
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: An esker is a fluvioglacial landform consisting of:
options: A frost-heaved patterned-ground feature
An unsorted ridge of till at the glacier margin
A steep-sided trough eroded by ice
A winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel deposited in a subglacial meltwater tunnel
questions.explain: Eskers are sinuous ridges of sorted sediment laid down by meltwater streams flowing within or beneath the ice.

questions.q: Within a coastal sediment cell, a source would be:
options: An offshore sediment sink
A cliff supplying material through erosion
A beach where sediment accumulates
A submarine canyon trapping sediment
questions.explain: Eroding cliffs and rivers supply sediment to the cell, acting as sources within the sediment budget.

questions.q: Longshore drift transports sediment along a coast because:
options: Swash approaches at an angle while backwash returns straight down the slope
Tidal currents move sediment offshore only
Waves always approach perpendicular to the shore
Backwash carries material directly back up the beach
questions.explain: Angled swash and gravity-driven perpendicular backwash move material in a zig-zag along the beach.

questions.q: An arete is best described as:
options: A flat-bottomed glacial trough
A knife-edged ridge between two corries
A mound of unsorted glacial till
A pyramidal peak
questions.explain: An arete is a sharp ridge formed where two corries erode back-to-back.

questions.q: In a cost-benefit analysis of coastal defence, a scheme is usually justified when:
options: The value of assets protected exceeds the cost of the defence
There are no inhabitants to protect
Costs greatly exceed benefits
Environmental impacts are ignored
questions.explain: Defences tend to be funded where the economic and social value protected outweighs construction and maintenance costs.

questions.q: A Shoreline Management Plan (SMP) policy of managed realignment means:
options: Building ever-larger sea walls
Holding the existing line at any cost
Allowing the coastline to retreat in a controlled way, often creating saltmarsh
Doing nothing at all
questions.explain: Managed realignment deliberately allows the shoreline to move landward, often restoring intertidal habitat.

questions.q: A ria (drowned river valley) is best classified as a feature of a:
options: Emergent coastline produced by isostatic uplift
Glacial trough
Submergent coastline produced by sea-level rise
Concordant rocky coast
questions.explain: Rias form when rising sea levels flood former river valleys, characteristic of submergent coastlines.

questions.q: Plucking as a glacial erosion process occurs when:
options: Frost shatters exposed rock above the ice
Rivers deposit sediment beneath the glacier
Rock debris embedded in ice scratches and grinds the bedrock
Meltwater refreezes onto bedrock and pulls fragments away as the ice moves
questions.explain: Plucking happens when meltwater freezes onto rock, and the moving ice tears loose blocks of bedrock.

questions.q: The periglacial process of frost heave produces:
options: Drumlin swarms
Striations on bedrock
Glacial troughs
Patterned ground through repeated freeze-thaw sorting of material
questions.explain: Frost heave repeatedly lifts and sorts stones, generating patterned ground in periglacial environments.

questions.q: A terminal moraine marks:
options: The lateral edge of a glacier
An area of frost-shattered rock
The maximum extent of a glacier's advance, deposited at its snout
A subglacial meltwater channel
questions.explain: A terminal moraine is the ridge of till deposited at the furthest point a glacier reached before retreat.

questions.q: The sequence cave, arch, stack, stump represents:
options: Progressive marine erosion of a resistant headland
Fluvioglacial landforms
Depositional landforms on a spit
Sub-aerial mass movement features
questions.explain: Marine erosion of weaknesses in a headland produces caves, then arches, stacks and finally stumps.

questions.q: A glacial system's mass balance is positive when:
options: The snout retreats rapidly
Ablation exceeds accumulation
Accumulation exceeds ablation, so the glacier advances
Inputs and outputs are equal
questions.explain: A positive mass (glacial) budget means more snow/ice is gained than lost, causing the glacier to advance.

questions.q: A U-shaped valley (glacial trough) differs from a river valley because glaciers:
options: Deposit material rather than erode
Erode laterally and vertically, widening and deepening into a steep-sided trough
Cannot transport large boulders
Erode only the valley floor, leaving an interlocking spur pattern
questions.explain: Glaciers erode both downwards and sideways, straightening and broadening valleys into steep-sided U-shapes.

questions.q: A raised beach is evidence of:
options: A submergent coastline
An emergent coastline caused by land rising relative to the sea
Marine transgression
Eustatic sea-level rise
questions.explain: Raised beaches sit above present sea level, indicating relative land emergence (e.g. isostatic rebound).

questions.q: Isostatic sea-level change refers to:
options: A change in the level of the land relative to the sea
A global rise in ocean water volume
The melting of continental ice sheets
Thermal expansion of seawater
questions.explain: Isostatic change is a local change in land level relative to the sea, e.g. post-glacial isostatic rebound.

questions.q: Abrasion differs from plucking in that abrasion:
options: Operates only in periglacial zones
Tears blocks of bedrock away by refreezing
Deposits till at the snout
Grinds and smooths bedrock using debris carried in the ice
questions.explain: Abrasion is the sandpaper-like wearing of bedrock by rock debris embedded in the moving ice.

questions.q: On a discordant coastline, the typical landform sequence is:
options: Continuous straight cliffs
Parallel offshore bars
A single concordant cove
Alternating headlands and bays due to differing rock resistance
questions.explain: Where rock bands meet the coast at right angles, resistant rock forms headlands and weaker rock forms bays.

questions.q: Eustatic sea-level change is best defined as:
options: Local subsidence from sediment compaction
A global change in the volume of water in the oceans
Tectonic uplift of a coastline
A change in the level of the land relative to the sea
questions.explain: Eustatic change is a worldwide change in sea level caused by changes in ocean water volume, e.g. from ice melt.

questions.q: A drumlin is a depositional landform that:
options: Has its blunt, steep end facing up-ice and tapers down-ice
Is steepest and blunt on the down-ice (lee) side
Forms a knife-edged ridge
Is composed of sorted outwash sand
questions.explain: Drumlins are streamlined till mounds with the blunt, steep end facing the ice flow and a tapered lee side.

questions.q: Hydraulic action as a marine erosion process operates by:
options: Rock fragments colliding and becoming rounded
The dissolving of calcium carbonate in seawater
Air compressed in joints by breaking waves, weakening the rock
The grinding of rock by sediment carried in waves
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is the force of water and trapped, compressed air shattering rock in cracks and joints.

questions.q: Which is a sub-aerial process operating on a cliff face?
options: Longshore drift
Hydraulic action
Marine deposition
Mass movement such as slumping
questions.explain: Sub-aerial processes (weathering and mass movement, e.g. slumping) act on the land above the wave zone.

questions.q: A corrie (cirque) is formed by:
options: Periglacial solifluction
Deposition of till at a glacier snout
Glacial erosion of a hollow on a mountainside, often armchair-shaped
Fluvioglacial outwash deposition
questions.explain: Corries are armchair-shaped hollows eroded by rotational ice movement, plucking and abrasion high on mountains.

questions.q: A spit forms where:
options: Wave refraction concentrates energy on a headland
Two headlands erode into a single bay
A river deposits a delta offshore
Longshore drift extends a ridge of deposited material across a bay or estuary
questions.explain: Spits develop where longshore drift carries sediment beyond a change in coastline orientation and deposits it.

questions.q: Fluvioglacial deposits differ from glacial till because they are:
options: Sorted and stratified by meltwater
Composed of wind-blown silt
Deposited directly by ice
Unsorted and angular
questions.explain: Fluvioglacial material is sorted and layered because meltwater rounds and grades the sediment.

questions.q: A groyne field can have a negative downdrift effect because it:
options: Prevents wave refraction
Increases longshore drift everywhere
Raises sea level locally
Traps sediment, starving beaches further along the coast
questions.explain: Groynes interrupt longshore drift, so beaches downdrift receive less sediment and may erode faster (terminal groyne effect).

questions.q: Constructive waves are associated with:
options: Steep wave fronts and rapid cliff retreat
High frequency, strong backwash and beach erosion
Removal of sediment offshore
Low frequency, strong swash and net deposition
questions.explain: Constructive waves have low frequency and a strong swash relative to backwash, building up the beach.

questions.q: Hard engineering at the coast differs from soft engineering in that it:
options: Uses built structures such as sea walls and groynes to resist the sea
Has no impact on sediment cells
Works with natural processes using beach nourishment
Always allows the coast to retreat
questions.explain: Hard engineering uses artificial structures to control erosion, whereas soft engineering works with natural processes.

questions.q: Till (boulder clay) is characterised as:
options: Wind-blown loess
Unsorted, angular material deposited directly by ice
Layered marine sediment
Well-sorted, rounded sediment deposited by meltwater
questions.explain: Till is unsorted, angular debris deposited directly by ice, in contrast to sorted fluvioglacial deposits.

questions.q: Integrated Coastal Zone Management (ICZM) is distinctive because it:
options: Ignores natural sediment cells
Focuses solely on hard engineering
Manages only a single town's seafront in isolation
Takes a holistic, long-term view of the whole coastal zone and its stakeholders
questions.explain: ICZM coordinates management across the entire coastal zone, balancing economic, social and environmental needs.

questions.q: Wave refraction at a headland causes:
options: Sediment to be removed from bays only
Equal energy along the whole coast
Wave energy to concentrate on the headland and dissipate in bays
Energy to spread out and weaken at the headland
questions.explain: Refraction bends waves so energy converges on headlands, encouraging erosion there and deposition in bays.
